opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it comes from looking at what happened with deep learning itself. For a long time, neural networks were this niche idea that a lot of people thought had hit a wall, and then it turned out that what they really needed was scale: more compute, more data, bigger models. Suddenly things that looked like toys started doing remarkable things. When I look at evolutionary methods and artificial life, I see a field that's in a pretty similar position. A lot of the classic experiments were run on tiny populations, small worlds, short time horizons, because that's all the hardware allowed. So I can't help wondering whether we've judged these ideas prematurely, the same way people once judged neural nets.

The other part is that I'm genuinely interested in open-endedness: systems that keep producing new and interesting things rather than converging on one answer and stopping. Natural evolution is the only existence proof we have of a process that does that, producing everything from bacteria to brains. Gradient descent on a fixed objective is incredibly powerful, but it's fundamentally about optimizing toward something you already specified. Evolution and artificial-life systems are much better at the exploratory side, at discovering stepping stones you didn't know you needed.

And now we finally have the tools to take that seriously. With accelerators and frameworks like JAX, you can simulate enormous populations in parallel, run worlds for far longer, and even use foundation models as part of the search, for example as mutation operators or as judges of what's interesting. So it feels like the right moment to ask what happens when you give these old ideas modern compute. Maybe nothing new happens. But if something does, if you get genuinely open-ended dynamics emerging at scale, that could be just as big a shift as what we saw with transformers. For me, that's too interesting a question not to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling evolutionary experiments with modern compute, but it does not compare spending hundreds of millions on the prevailing AI approach with spending only tens of thousands on the largest evolution-based searches.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, part of it is honestly just that I find it fascinating. I think if you look at the history of how we got intelligence in the first place, there was only ever one process that we know of that actually produced it, and that's evolution. So it seems a little strange to me that the field has put almost all of its effort into one particular path, which is gradient descent on big transformers, and relatively little into the one process that we know works.

And the other thing is, when I think about what deep learning has actually taught us over the last ten or fifteen years, the big lesson is that when you take simple ideas and you throw compute at them, things that didn't look like they worked suddenly start working. Neural networks were around for decades and people had largely written them off. Evolutionary methods and artificial life feel very much like they're in that pre-scaling phase. The experiments people are doing are mostly tiny, you run them on a laptop, and then people conclude it doesn't work. I don't think we've actually tested that. Nobody has really put a data center behind an open-ended evolutionary system and seen what happens.

There's also a more philosophical reason, which is that I'm a bit uncomfortable with how much of current AI is us hand-designing things. We design the architecture, we design the training objective, we curate the data, we design the benchmarks. Everything is top-down. Evolution and artificial life are the opposite of that. You set up an environment and some rules and you let the system find things you didn't think of. And I think the really interesting ideas, the ones that would actually surprise us, are much more likely to come from a process like that than from me sitting down and sketching a new attention variant. Transformers were a nice idea, but I'd like the next step to be something we discover rather than something we draw on a whiteboard.

And finally, it's sort of a more collective approach to intelligence that interests me. Nature doesn't build one giant brain, it builds lots of smaller things that interact, compete, cooperate. I suspect there's a lot to learn from that at scale, and we just haven't looked properly yet.

r001.rationale: The response says most effort goes to gradient descent and that evolutionary experiments are mostly tiny, but it does not state the specified spending contrast of hundreds of millions of dollars versus tens of thousands.

astra-6.text:
What interests me is that evolution is the one process we know of that produced intelligence, and it didn’t start with intelligence as an explicit objective. It emerged from organisms interacting with their environment and with each other. That suggests there’s something worth exploring beyond optimizing a model against a task we’ve already specified.

With artificial life, I’d like to see how far you can get with simple rules and enough room for things to develop. Can organisms create new challenges for one another? Can you get an environment where becoming more capable keeps being useful, rather than reaching a fixed solution and stopping?

Scaling is interesting because a small experiment that settles down quickly doesn’t necessarily tell you what happens with much larger populations, richer interactions, and longer runs. But I don’t think simply throwing compute at it guarantees anything. The difficult part is finding conditions that support continuing innovation. That’s the question I find exciting: can we build a system that keeps producing interesting things we didn’t explicitly ask it to produce?

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling evolutionary experiments and compute, but it does not compare spending hundreds of millions on prevailing AI with tens of thousands on evolution-based searches.

sol-6.1.text:
What interests me is that evolution gives us a way to discover things we wouldn’t know how to design directly. With most machine learning, we choose the architecture, the objective, and quite a lot of the structure of the problem. That’s incredibly useful, but it also constrains what you can find.

With artificial life, you can ask a slightly different question: what conditions allow interesting behavior to emerge and keep getting more complex? Can you get agents that develop new strategies, interact with each other, and create new problems for each other to solve?

Scaling those experiments is exciting because a small experiment might miss precisely the dynamics you’re interested in. But I don’t think compute alone is the answer. You need an environment where novelty can actually matter, rather than a system that just finds one clever exploit and stops. That combination—more scale and the right conditions for open-ended discovery—is what I find compelling.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling evolutionary experiments and contrasts them with conventional machine learning, but it does not compare spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the prevailing AI approach with spending only tens of thousands on the largest evolution-based searches.
